extracted.intended_audience: researchers and clinicians conducting systematic reviews/meta-analyses of psychological interventions (positive psychology researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of positive psychology interventions (PPIs) assessing effects on subjective well-being, psychological well-being, and depression, with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, quality assessment, and meta-analytic procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Positive Psychology Intervention (PPI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive psychology intervention (PPI) was defined in accordance with Sin and Lyubomirsky’s (2009) article as a psychological intervention (training, exercise, therapy) primarily aimed at raising positive feelings, positive cognitions or positive behavior as opposed to interventions aiming to reduce symptoms, problems or disorders. The intervention should have been explicitly developed in line with the theoretical tradition of positive psychology (usually reported in the introduction section of an article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of PPIs include counting your blessings, practicing kindness, setting personal goals, expressing gratitude and using personal strengths. Interventions not explicitly grounded in positive psychology (e.g., mindfulness, life-review) were excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies had to: examine the effects of a PPI; use randomization of study subjects (individuals, not groups); include a comparator condition (no intervention, placebo, care as usual); be published in a peer-reviewed journal; measure at least one outcome of well-being (subjective and/or psychological) or depression (diagnosis or symptoms); and report sufficient statistics to enable calculation of standardized effect sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, authors were contacted for supplementary data. The search and inclusion were restricted to peer-reviewed studies in the English language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study exclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluded studies involved physical exercises aimed at improvement of well-being, mindfulness or meditation interventions, forgiveness therapy, life-review and reminiscence interventions, and well-being interventions in diseased populations not explicitly grounded in positive psychology theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: these intervention types were beyond the scope of the meta-analysis or had separate extensive meta-analyses available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization unit requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomization of the study subjects (randomizing individuals, not groups) was required for inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures comparability across conditions and aligns with the study's focus on individual RCTs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparator condition requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Included studies must have a comparator condition such as no intervention, a placebo intervention, waiting list, or another active intervention (care as usual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparator types are explicitly enumerated and used to classify included trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary outcome domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary outcomes for the meta-analysis were subjective well-being (SWB), psychological well-being (PWB) and depressive symptoms/depression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple instruments measured the same domain (e.g., several SWB scales), the mean of the effect sizes was calculated so each study contributed one effect size per outcome domain. Instruments explicitly measuring depression (e.g., BDI, CES-D) were used for depression effect sizes; related constructs (e.g., positive affect for SWB, hope for PWB) were used for well-being outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient statistics requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies had to report sufficient statistics to enable the calculation of standardized effect sizes (Cohen's d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, study authors were contacted to obtain missing data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic search strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic literature search was carried out in PsycInfo, PubMed and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for the period 1998 to November 2012 using MeSH terms and text words: 'well-being' or 'happiness' or 'happy*', 'optimism', 'positive psychology' combined with 'intervention','treatment','therapy','prevention' and outcome terms 'effect*' or 'effic*' or 'outcome*' or 'evaluat*'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searches were complemented by cross-checking references from retrieved studies and prior meta-analyses/reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study selection procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Two reviewers independently selected potentially eligible studies in two phases: screening titles/abstracts first and full-text in the second phase. All studies identified as potentially eligible by at least one reviewer in phase one were re-assessed in phase two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter-rater reliability (kappa) was reported (0.90); disagreements were resolved by consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data extraction procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Data extraction and study quality assessment were performed by one reviewer and independently checked by a second reviewer; disagreements were resolved by consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extracted data included design, intervention characteristics, target group, recruitment methods, delivery mode, number of sessions, attrition rates, control group, outcome measures and effect sizes (post-test and follow-up >=3 months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment criteria: randomization concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequacy of randomization concealment was one of six quality criteria used to assess methodological quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each criterion was rated 0 (does not meet) or 1 (meets); inter-rater reliability (kappa) for quality ratings was 0.91.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment criteria: blinding of subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Blinding of subjects to the study condition (where applicable) was assessed as a quality criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blinding of assessors was noted as often not applicable in these studies; each criterion scored 0/1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment criteria: baseline comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline comparability: whether study groups were comparable at baseline and whether this was explicitly assessed (or adjustments were made to correct baseline imbalance using appropriate covariates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0/1 as part of the six-item scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment criteria: power analysis or N>=50
rubrics_metrics.description: Power analysis: presence of an adequate power analysis and/or whether there were at least 50 participants in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counted as one binary quality item (0/1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment criteria: completeness of follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Completeness of follow up data: clear attrition analysis and loss to follow up < 50%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0/1; attrition reporting influences quality score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality assessment criteria: handling of missing data (intention-to-treat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Handling of missing data: use of intention-to-treat analysis (as opposed to completers-only analysis) was assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0/1; very few studies conducted intention-to-treat analyses in this set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study quality summary scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite study quality score was the sum of the six binary quality criteria (range 0–6). Studies were classified as high quality when five or six criteria were met, medium when three or four criteria were met, and low when zero, one or two criteria were met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Along with a summary score, individual quality aspects were also considered because composite quality scales can be equivocal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect size calculation (Cohen's d) procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect sizes (Cohen’s d) were calculated by subtracting the average score of the experimental group (Me) from the average score of the control group (Mc) and dividing by the pooled standard deviation. If baseline differences existed despite randomization, d's were calculated based on standardized pre-post change scores for experimental and control groups and Δd = de – dc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more than one measure was used for an outcome, the mean of the effect sizes was calculated so that each study outcome had one effect size. If a study had more than one experimental group compared with one control, the number of subjects in the control group was evenly divided across experimental groups so each subject was used only once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation thresholds for effect sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: From a clinical perspective the authors used thresholds for Cohen's d: effects of 0.56–1.2 interpreted as large, 0.33–0.55 as medium, and 0–0.32 as small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thresholds are cited to aid interpretation of pooled effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis model choice
rubrics_metrics.description: A random effects model was chosen a priori because of the expected diversity of studies and populations; a common effect size was not assumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random effects outcomes are conservative (wider 95% CIs). Analyses were performed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA, Version 2.2.064).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlier handling policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Outliers were considered but not automatically removed; the a priori planned exclusion criterion was Cohen’s d > 2.5 from the final sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The usual outlier-removal procedure (removing studies outside pooled CI) is advised when a common effect size is assumed, but because high dispersion was expected the authors planned minimal exclusion. Removing outliers was shown to reduce heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q-statistic and the I2-statistic. I2 is a percentage indicating study-to-study dispersion due to real differences over and above sampling error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation guidance: I2 = 0% indicates absence of dispersion; 25% low; 50% moderate; 75% high heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderator/subgroup analyses (pre-specified moderators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Six potential moderators examined were: (1) self-selected sample vs not self-selected, (2) duration (less than four weeks / four to eight weeks / more than eight weeks), (3) type of intervention (self-help, group, individual therapy), (4) recruitment method (community, internet, referral/hospital, university), (5) presence of psychosocial problems (yes/none), and (6) study quality rating (low/medium/high).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The impact of duration and quality ratings was also assessed using meta-regression. Subgroup analyses were used to test differences in Cohen's d between subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-selection moderator definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-selected sample / not self-selected: did the participants know that the aim of the intervention was to make them feel better?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to classify studies and investigate whether participant self-selection moderated effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration subgroup categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration categories used for subgrouping interventions: less than four weeks; four to eight weeks; or more than eight weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration was treated as a potential moderator and entered into meta-regression analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication bias assessment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication bias was assessed with funnel plots, Orwin's fail-safe number and the Trim and Fill method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orwin's fail-safe number indicates number of non-significant unpublished studies needed to reduce overall effect to non-significance; an effect size is considered robust if the number required exceeds 5K + 10 (K = number of included studies). Trim and Fill imputes missing studies to restore funnel plot symmetry and yields an adjusted pooled effect size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up analysis inclusion rule
rubrics_metrics.description: For follow-up analyses the authors included effect sizes at follow up of at least 3 months (and up to 12 months); for interpretation they focused on effects from 3 to 6 months as short-term follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up outcome extraction required minimum 3-month interval to be included in follow-up meta-analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting of the meta-analysis results followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRISMA was explicitly applied for transparent reporting of search, selection, and synthesis.
